decisions.proposedPhrase: Grainy chocolate always means bad temper.
decisions.reason: Other causes exist; texture alone does not diagnose polymorphism.
Ordinary physical remelting need not change recipe; overheating/oxidation are separate.
Tempering governs crystallization; seed chocolate must be composition-compatible when claiming identical recipe.
Controlled processing can recover useful properties; bad is vague and not a food-safety conclusion.

decisions.proposedPhrase: There is one correct cocoa-butter crystal, and Form V always guarantees perfect chocolate.
decisions.reason: Form V is generally targeted, not sufficient; quality depends on network/formulation.
Bloom can cause white surfaces; this does not certify that any real sample is safe or mold-free.

decisions.proposedPhrase: Fat bloom and sugar bloom are the same.
decisions.reason: Fat and sugar components differ; coexistence does not make them identical.

decisions.proposedPhrase: Tempering is simply cooling chocolate slowly.
decisions.reason: Temperature management and suitable nucleation/structure matter; no single cooling speed defines tempering.
Metaphor only; surviving seeds and kinetics explain thermal-history effects.

decisions.proposedPhrase: The same ingredients guarantee the same material structure.
decisions.reason: Composition constrains possibilities but processing changes structure.

decisions.proposedPhrase: A universal molecular explanation and damage temperature explains every case of overheated chocolate.
decisions.reason: Excessive heat is a separate possible damage route, not proved to be merely poor temper. Exact degradation threshold/mechanism requires further research; excluded from narration.

decisions.proposedPhrase: A future Magnivis melt-and-reset demonstration will visibly prove its samples have different cocoa-butter polymorphs.
decisions.reason: No demonstration performed. Snap/gloss alone cannot identify polymorphs; instrumented evidence required. Original schematic can explain, not claim experimental proof.
